prompt: Using the formula busy ÷ (1 − busy), how many days of waiting does a person at 80% busy produce, for work of one day on average?
By the same formula, what is the wait at 95% busy, in days?
Which two things together make waiting explode near 100% busy?

choices.text: Lazy people and bad tools
choices.why: The curve appears with diligent people and good tools.

choices.text: Too many meetings and too few deployments
choices.why: Neither is in the simulation, and the curve is there.

choices.text: Variability and no slack
choices.why: Right. Remove either and the curve flattens.

choices.text: Large items and small teams
choices.why: Size shifts the scale; the explosion comes from variability without room.

prompt: Why did the Billing team's review queue in July behave like the curve's right-hand end?

choices.text: One person, almost no time to spare
choices.why: Right. Her review capacity was small and fully used, so items waited days for an hour's work.

choices.text: Reviews took several days each
choices.why: Reviews took hours; the days were queueing.

choices.text: Developers stopped sending items to review
choices.why: They kept sending; that was the queue.

choices.text: The pipeline only ran on Thursdays
choices.why: That affected deployment, after review.

prompt: Why does queue.py's simulated wait at 90% come out lower than the formula's 9 days?

choices.text: The formula is wrong above 80%
choices.why: The formula holds; the simulation is a sample.

choices.text: The program has a bug at 90%
choices.why: Nothing is wrong; another seed would land elsewhere.

choices.text: People work faster when busy
choices.why: Work time is drawn the same way at every level.

choices.text: Still only a sample
choices.why: Right. Near the top of the curve, samples vary a lot.

prompt: Five people work five days a week. Holidays and illness take 2.5 days, meetings 2.5, reviews 2.5, on-call 2.0 and support 1.5. How many days are left for planned items?
Why does a throughput-based forecast already allow for meetings, reviews and incidents?

choices.text: Because the program subtracts them
choices.why: It subtracts nothing; it does not need to.

choices.text: Throughput is measured after all of them
choices.why: Right. The history has already done the subtraction.

choices.text: Because meetings are counted as items
choices.why: Only work items are counted.

choices.text: It does not; they must be added by hand
choices.why: They are inside every day of the history.

prompt: Why does a ten-minute support question cost more than ten minutes?

choices.text: Because support is billed by the hour
choices.why: Billing is not the cost here.

choices.text: Because it must be logged in a ticket
choices.why: Logging takes a minute.

choices.text: Getting back into work costs time
choices.why: Right. The interruption costs the switch back, lesson 4.

choices.text: Because support questions are always hard
choices.why: Many are easy; the cost is the switch.

prompt: Which are cheap ways to measure how much capacity goes to unplanned work? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Label unplanned items when they arrive
choices.why: Right. Then count them.

choices.text: Compare what was planned with what was done over a quarter
choices.why: Right. The unplanned share is next quarter's planning number.

choices.text: Ask each developer to log their hours by the minute
choices.why: Expensive, resented, and not needed for this.

choices.text: Count incidents and support requests per week
choices.why: Right. Simple counts are enough.

prompt: Tom DeMarco's 2001 book arguing that organisations need room to respond is called ___.
What does slack mean in this lesson?

choices.text: Planned work that leaves room
choices.why: Right. Room used when it is needed: the urgent, a review, an improvement.

choices.text: People with nothing to do
choices.why: Slack is room in the plan, not idle people.

choices.text: A longer deadline added secretly
choices.why: That is padding, which lesson 11 rejects.

choices.text: Time off after a hard quarter
choices.why: Rest matters, and it is a different thing.

prompt: "We cannot afford people who are not busy." What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: That slack is free
choices.why: It costs capacity; the point is what it buys.

choices.text: That busy people are less productive
choices.why: The argument is about queues, not individuals.

choices.text: That the team should hire more people
choices.why: Hiring is not the answer the lesson gives.

choices.text: It is paid already, in waiting
choices.why: Right. Paid by the requester, later, as lead time.

prompt: Where does slack matter most?

choices.text: In the newest member of the team
choices.why: Slack is about steps in the flow, not people.

choices.text: At the bottleneck
choices.why: Right. In July that was review.

choices.text: In the backlog
choices.why: The backlog is a queue, not a capacity.

choices.text: Equally everywhere
choices.why: The step everything waits for gains most.

prompt: Put the lesson's steps for planning a quarter in order.
items: order the rest below a line

prompt: A Monte Carlo forecast says 85% of quarters finish at least 80 items. Planning to 75% of that, how many items should be committed?
What does a spreadsheet allocating every person at exactly 100% hide?

choices.text: Who is working on what
choices.why: That is exactly what it shows.

choices.text: The team's total salary
choices.why: Salary is not the issue.

choices.text: That no room is left for a surprise
choices.why: Right. The first incident is taken from somebody's 100%, and a project slips undecided.

choices.text: Which projects are most important
choices.why: Priorities can be shown beside it.

prompt: Why does adding people to a late project usually make it later?

choices.text: They cut capacity before adding it
choices.why: Right. They need time and take time from those already productive.

choices.text: New people are less skilled
choices.why: Skill is not the argument; ramp-up and coordination are.

choices.text: Projects cannot use more than five people
choices.why: No such limit.

choices.text: Brooks proved it is always true
choices.why: It is a strong tendency, described in 1975, not a proof.

prompt: When is adding people the right move?

choices.text: To recover a date next month
choices.why: Too late to pay back the ramp-up.

choices.text: Whenever the queue is long
choices.why: Often the queue needs capacity at one step, not new people.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: It is right for a team that needs more capacity for years.

choices.text: If it is needed for years
choices.why: Right. Not as a fix for a near date.

prompt: Match each level of busyness to the approximate wait queue.py measured.
A manager proposes raising the team's utilisation from 75% to 95% to deliver more. What does the curve predict?

choices.text: A quarter more output and nothing else
choices.why: Output may rise a little; waiting rises a lot.

choices.text: Much longer waits for every request
choices.why: Right. From about 3 days to about 19 by the formula.

choices.text: Shorter waits, because more gets done
choices.why: The opposite: there is no room left to absorb variation.

choices.text: No change, because the team is the same
choices.why: The load changed, and the curve is about load.

prompt: Using busy ÷ (1 − busy), how many times longer is the wait at 90% busy than at 60%?
Two teams finish the same number of items. One runs at 70% busy, the other at 95%. Which statement fits the lesson?

choices.text: The 95% team is more efficient and should be the model
choices.why: Its requesters wait far longer for the same output.

choices.text: Both serve their requesters equally
choices.why: Equal output, very unequal waiting.

choices.text: The 70% team answers requests much sooner
choices.why: Right. Same throughput, a fraction of the queue.

choices.text: The 70% team must be overstaffed
choices.why: Its slack is what keeps waits short and absorbs the unplanned.
